title: Bricks Without Straw: The First Demand Backfires
summary: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go into the wilderness to hold a feast to the LORD. Pharaoh answers that he does not know the LORD and orders that the slaves gather their own straw while still making the same number of bricks. The Israelite foremen are beaten, blame Moses and Aaron, and Moses takes his bewildered complaint to God.
story: Chapter 4 ended with the elders believing and worshiping. Chapter 5 is the first meeting with Pharaoh, and it goes about as badly as it could. The request is modest, the answer is contempt, and the people Moses came to rescue end up worse off than before. Pharaoh's question in verse 2, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?” sets the agenda for the next ten chapters, which are God's answer to it. The chapter also teaches something the rest of the Bible repeats: the first result of obeying God can be more suffering, not less. Moses' complaint at the end leads straight into God's reply in chapter 6, where he restates his name and his promises.
historical:
Pharaoh's building programs depended on masses of conscripted labor. Egypt built its temples and tombs in stone, but houses, palaces, storehouses, and fortress walls were made of mudbrick: Nile mud mixed with chopped straw or chaff, pressed into wooden molds, and dried in the sun. The straw helped bind the clay so the bricks held together as they dried. A well-known painting in the tomb of Rekhmire, vizier (chief minister) under Thutmose III in the fifteenth century BC, shows foreign laborers drawing water, mixing mud, molding bricks, and stacking them under the eye of overseers, for the building works of the temple of Amun. Exodus 1:11 places Israel's labor on the store cities of Pithom and Rameses in the eastern Nile Delta. Egyptian administrative documents from the New Kingdom record brick quotas for work gangs, so a daily tally of bricks, as in verses 8 and 14, fits what is known of how such work was run.

The chain of command in verses 6 to 19 also rings true. Egyptian taskmasters stood over the work force, and under them were Israelite foremen, drawn from the enslaved people themselves, who kept the tallies and answered for any shortfall. Their position was the cruelest: responsible to Pharaoh for the numbers, trusted by neither side, and beaten when the quota was missed. The same Hebrew word for these officials later names the officers who helped Moses and Joshua organize the people (Numbers 11:16; Joshua 1:10).
cultural:
Pharaoh's answer made sense in his world. Egypt had many gods, and the king himself was regarded as divine, the son of the sun god and the living Horus. The god of a slave people, whose name he had never heard, had no claim on him. Asking leave to worship was not strange in itself, but the verb for holding a feast in verse 1 is the one Israel later used for its pilgrimage festivals, the three feasts a year when the people went up to appear before the LORD (Exodus 23:14-17). Worship in this chapter means going somewhere and offering sacrifice, and chapter 8 will explain why it could not be done inside Egypt. Pharaoh reads the whole request as idleness: “For they are lazy” (verse 8). To a system that measures people by output, devotion looks like wasted time, and his answer is to make the work so heavy that no one has breath left to think about their God.

When the foremen tell Moses and Aaron “you have made us a stench before Pharaoh” (verse 21), they use a Hebrew idiom for becoming hateful to someone. Jacob uses the same image when he complains that Simeon and Levi have made him a stench to the Canaanites (Genesis 34:30). The foremen go further: Moses has put a sword in Pharaoh's hand. In a society where the king's favor meant life, being made offensive to him was a death sentence waiting to be carried out.
literary: The chapter is built as a chain of messages, running down and then back up. God's word goes through Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh; Pharaoh's word goes through the taskmasters and foremen to the people; then the foremen carry their protest back to Pharaoh, turn on Moses and Aaron, and Moses carries it up to God. Two messenger formulas collide. Moses opens with “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says” (verse 1), and a few verses later the taskmasters announce “This is what Pharaoh says” (verse 10). The question of the whole plague narrative is which king's word will stand. Pharaoh's “I do not know the LORD” (verse 2) is answered again and again in the chapters ahead, where God acts so that Egypt and Israel will know that he is the LORD. The Hebrew root for work and service also runs through the chapter, since the same root is used for slave labor and for worship. The chapter ends without resolution, in Moses' raw question in verses 22 and 23, which takes the form of many psalms of lament: why, Lord?

outline.t: Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh: who is the LORD?
The foremen appeal to Pharaoh and turn on Moses
Moses takes his complaint to the LORD

doctrines.note: Pharaoh's question, “Who is the LORD?” is the question Exodus sets out to answer. God does not reply with an argument but with acts, and the chapters that follow are his self-introduction to Egypt and to Israel.

Obedience makes things worse before it makes them better. The chapter is honest that faithful action can bring immediate harm, and that God's timing can feel like absence. The foremen's anger and Moses' complaint are recorded without a word of rebuke.

Moses brings his confusion straight to God: “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me?” (verse 22). Scripture treats this kind of lament as faith speaking honestly, not as unbelief, and God answers it in the next chapter.

words.note: Yada, to know. The word covers more than information. It is knowledge by acquaintance and experience, and it can include acknowledging someone's authority. When Pharaoh says “I do not know the LORD” (verse 2), he means both that he has never heard of this god and that he does not recognize his claim. The plague chapters answer with a refrain built on the same verb: they will know that I am the LORD (for example 6:7, 7:5, and 7:17).

Avodah, work or service. It names the crushing labor Pharaoh imposes (verse 9), and its root gives the verb for serving or worshiping God. The contest in Exodus is over whom Israel will serve, and Pharaoh increases the service he demands at the very moment the LORD asks for his people to serve him.

Shoter, an official or officer, translated foremen in this chapter. These were Israelites set over their fellow slaves to keep the brick count, caught between Egyptian taskmasters and their own people. The word later names the officers who helped organize Israel in the wilderness and in the conquest.

christ: Stephen's speech in Acts reads Moses' career as a pattern: “This Moses, whom they had rejected” is the one God sent to be Israel's ruler and redeemer (Acts 7:35). Chapter 5 is the first time Moses' own people turn against him, and it will not be the last. The New Testament sees the same pattern fulfilled in Jesus, of whom John writes, “He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him” (John 1:11). There is a second, thematic contrast. Pharaoh answers the cry of worn-out slaves by making their burden heavier. Jesus answers it the other way: “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Exodus does not predict that saying, but it shows the kind of master Jesus is not, and the kind of rescue the whole Bible is moving toward, from a king who crushes to one who gives rest.

hard.q: Was Moses' request for a short trip to worship a deception, since God meant to bring Israel out for good?
hard.a:
God told Moses to ask for exactly this (3:18), and in chapter 5 Moses asks for a feast in the wilderness and a three-day trip to sacrifice, not for permanent release. Yet God had already said he would bring Israel out of Egypt and into Canaan (3:8, 17). Readers have handled the tension in several ways. Many see the request as a genuine but modest first demand that exposes Pharaoh's heart: if he will not grant slaves a few days to worship their God, he will certainly not free them, and his refusal justifies what follows. Others stress that the request was true as far as it went. The first goal God named was worship at the mountain (3:12), and the break with Egypt becomes complete because Pharaoh escalates, not because Moses lied. A third group grants that the request held back the full intention and compares it with other places where the Old Testament shows the weak outwitting a murderous power, such as the Hebrew midwives in 1:15-21, noting that the text records the tactic without praising or condemning it.

Whichever view one takes, the chapter makes clear that Pharaoh's objection was never about the length of the trip. He rejects any claim the LORD has on his slaves, and he answers even the smallest request with a heavier yoke.

questions: Pharaoh treats the request to worship as proof of laziness. Where does our own culture treat rest, prayer, or worship as wasted time?
The Israelite foremen were trapped between the taskmasters and their own people. Where have you seen people squeezed in the middle of an unjust system, and what do they need from those around them?
Moses takes his confusion straight to God. What keeps you from praying as honestly as he does in verses 22 and 23?
